subject: Computer Networking
title: HTTP: How Browsers Talk to Servers
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: HTTP: How Browsers Talk to Servers.

hook.text: Every time you load a page, your browser and a server exchange messages in a language called HTTP.

buildup.text: HTTP defines methods: GET fetches data, POST sends data, PUT updates, DELETE removes. Simple verbs.

discovery.text: Each response includes a status code. 200 means success. 404 means not found. 500 means server error.

twist.text: HTTP is stateless — the server forgets you after each request. Cookies and sessions add memory on top.

climax.text: HTTPS adds encryption. Without it, anyone on the same network could read your HTTP traffic in plain text.

punchline.text: HTTP is the language of the web. HTTPS makes it private.

quiz.question: What does 'stateless' mean in the context of HTTP?
options: The server doesn't remember previous requests
The server has no physical location
Data is never stored on disk

details.summary: HTTP is the protocol browsers use to request and receive web content. It uses a simple request-response pattern with methods like GET and POST. HTTP is stateless, meaning each request is independent. Headers carry metadata and the body carries content like HTML, JSON, or images.
details.whyItMatters: HTTP is the foundation of the web. Every web page, API call, and file download uses HTTP. Understanding it unlocks debugging, performance optimization, and API design.
takeaways: HTTP uses request-response with methods like GET and POST
Each request is stateless and independent
Headers carry metadata; the body carries content

faq.question: Why is HTTP stateless?
faq.answer: Statelessness simplifies servers because they do not need to track client connections between requests. Each request contains all information needed to process it. Cookies and sessions add state on top of stateless HTTP when applications need to track users across requests.

faq.question: What is the difference between GET and POST?
faq.answer: GET requests data without changing anything on the server. POST sends data to create or modify a resource. GET parameters are visible in the URL. POST data is in the request body. Browsers can safely retry GET requests but not POST, because POST may cause side effects.
